name: The Norway Maple of Herrnstraße
story:
Munich protects this maple for being big, which says more about the species than about the tree. Acer platanoides is among the most planted street trees in Europe and among the most frequently cut back: fast, cheap, tolerant of road salt, compacted soil and bad air, and generally treated as replaceable. The city's 2021 natural monument ordinance takes the opposite line here, entering it as stadtbildwirksam, effective in the townscape, and rare at this size within the city. That is a statute saying a common tree becomes an uncommon one simply by being left alone.

It stands on Herrnstraße in the Lehel, the grid of tall nineteenth century blocks laid out between the old town wall and the Isar when Munich first built beyond its gates. This is dense inner city: courtyards, parked cars, five storeys on both sides, and one crown holding the middle of it.

If you want to be certain what you are looking at, snap a leaf stalk. A Norway maple bleeds white, and the sycamore it is constantly mistaken for does not. In April it flowers before it leafs, and the bare crown turns acid yellow-green for a fortnight.

The ordinance records why a tree is protected and never when it was planted. No dated source exists for this one, so how long it has stood here is not known.

best_time.label: April, when it flowers before it leafs and the bare crown turns acid yellow-green

name: The Beech of the Wilhelmsgymnasium
transport: 1 min walk from the Maxmonument bus stop
story:
The school across this green space has been teaching since 1559, which makes it the oldest in Munich. The beech below it carries no recorded date of any kind, and the city protects it anyway. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance enters it as a mighty, dominant tree, effective in the streetscape, and that is the entire reasoning.

Fagus sylvatica behaves badly in cities, which is why a full grown one in the Lehel is worth the detour. It wants deep, moist, well drained ground, it resents compacted soil, and its bark is thin and smooth enough to scald in full sun where a rough barked oak would shrug. Given room it becomes the most dominant broadleaf in central Europe: the shade under a mature beech is close to total, almost nothing germinates in it, and the floor stays bare leaf litter year after year. That is how the species took most of the continent's forests.

The Wilhelmsgymnasium moved into its building on the corner in 1877, a Jesuit foundation by then three centuries into its second life as a state school. The green strip on its south side is the sort of leftover municipal ground that usually holds bins and a bike rack.

No age is on record. The ordinance lists reasons for protection and carries no column for dates or dimensions, and nothing else has measured this tree.

best_time.label: late October and November, when the crown turns copper over the green in front of the school

name: The Horse Chestnut of St.-Anna-Platz
story:
Munich's beer gardens are chestnut groves for an engineering reason. Brewers dug cellars along the Isar to hold beer through the summer and planted horse chestnuts over them, because the species throws heavy shade from shallow roots that will not force their way into a vault. Then they discovered that people would rather drink under the trees than carry the beer home, and the beer garden existed.

This one shades no cellar. It stands at the southwest corner of St.-Anna-Platz in the Lehel, between two churches of very different temperament: the small Klosterkirche finished in 1733, generally counted the first rococo church built in Old Bavaria, and the far larger parish church that went up beside it in the 1890s. Both were gutted by bombing and rebuilt.

The 2021 natural monument ordinance protects the tree as platzbildprägend, defining the square, and calls it mighty and healthy. Healthy is the word to notice. Since the 1990s the horse chestnut leaf miner, a moth out of the Balkans, has browned and curled the foliage of chestnuts across Europe by mid July, so a chestnut still carrying green leaves in August is doing better than most of its species.

Its age is not on record anywhere. The ordinance gives reasons and no dates, and nothing else has measured this tree.

best_time.label: May, when it puts up white candles over the benches on the square

name: The Hackberry of the Luitpoldpark
story:
The hill in this park is what was left of Munich after 1945. From 1946 onward the rubble of the bombed city was carted up to Schwabing and piled into the Luitpoldhügel, roughly 37 metres of broken masonry now buried under grass and footpaths, with a view across to the Olympic Park from the top.

The park underneath it is older. It was laid out in 1911, when 90 lime trees went in for the ninetieth birthday of Prince Regent Luitpold. The hackberry is not one of them. Celtis australis belongs to southern Europe, Asia Minor and North Africa, its natural range stopping well south of the Alps, and Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance calls it an extremely rare species in the city, protected here for being beautiful and for an interesting growth form rather than for any size.

It was the timber of whip handles, pitchforks and walking sticks, chosen because it bends a long way before it breaks. The quickest way to be sure you have found one is the leaf: lopsided at the base, one half running further down the stalk than the other, with a hard toothed edge. The fruit is a small dark drupe, sweet and almost entirely stone.

The ordinance records why the tree is protected, never when it was planted, and no age exists for it anywhere.

name: The Amur Cork Tree of the Luitpoldpark
transport: 3 min walk from the Ackermannstraße tram stop
story:
You can press a thumb into this tree and the bark gives. The Amur cork tree carries a thick, soft, deeply ridged corky layer that dents under a hand and springs back, which is exactly why Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it for an interesting bark pattern and calls the species extremely rare in the city.

Phellodendron amurense comes from the Amur river country on the Russian and Chinese border, and from Korea and northern Japan, which is a continental climate with harder winters than Bavaria has ever managed. Under the cork the inner bark is a startling sulphur yellow, and it is one of the fundamental herbs of Chinese medicine. The leaves are pinnate, like an ash, and turn clear yellow in autumn; the berries are black and smell of turpentine when crushed. In the northeastern United States the same tree seeds itself so aggressively into hardwood forest that several states have banned its sale. In a Schwabing park it just stands there being unusual.

The ground it stands on is the Luitpoldpark, laid out in 1911 and dominated by a hill made from the rubble of the bombed city. A Mediterranean hackberry, protected under the same ordinance for the same rarity, grows about 200 metres east.

The ordinance lists reasons and carries no dates or measurements, so the tree's age is unknown.

name: The Horse Chestnut of the Gasteig
transport: 1 min walk from the Am Gasteig tram stop
story:
Gasteig comes from gacher Steig, steep path, and that is the whole explanation of this corner of Munich. The ground drops away here to the Isar, so everything on the slope has had to be terraced, buttressed or built into the bank, and the horse chestnut stands at the top of the fall. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it as a striking, wide-spreading tree, particularly effective in the streetscape.

Wide-spreading is the phrase worth stopping on. A street chestnut is normally cut back into a lollipop to keep it clear of the trams, the wires and the upper windows, and it spends its life as half a crown. This one has been left to throw its lower limbs out sideways, which is what the species does when nobody interferes.

Its neighbour is the Gasteig itself, the concert hall that opened in 1985 as home of the Munich Philharmonic and emptied out in 2021 for a rebuild, the orchestra decamping to a converted industrial hall across the river. The tree stayed where it was.

The species is not local either. Aesculus hippocastanum is native to a handful of mountain ravines in Greece and Albania, where it is a threatened tree, and planted by the million everywhere else. No age is recorded here: Munich's ordinance says why a tree is protected and never how old it is.

best_time.label: September and October, when the conkers ripen and drop along the pavement

name: The Horse Chestnut of Edlingerstraße
story:
The word Munich's ordinance uses for this tree is Solitär, which in the trade means a tree with open ground on every side and therefore the shape the species actually has. Almost no street tree gets that. They go in as rows, get pruned away from windows and cables, and end up as half a crown facing the road. This chestnut got the room, and the 2021 natural monument ordinance says as much: a solitary, beautiful and evenly grown tree, very dominant in the streetscape.

It stands where Sommerstraße meets Edlingerstraße in the Au, the low quarter on the flood plain of the Isar that spent centuries being washed out by the river and just as long being the poorest district in Munich. A few streets away, Mariahilfplatz has hosted the Auer Dult three times a year since 1905, a crockery and junk fair whose market privileges run back to the eighteenth century.

An evenly grown horse chestnut is a specific thing to stand under: a dome that starts low and closes to a point, carried on limbs that sweep down before turning back up at the tips. In May the whole of it goes up in white candles, each flower marked with a yellow blotch that turns red once it has been pollinated, so the tree is telling the bees which ones are already finished.

No age is on record.

best_time.label: May, when the whole dome goes up in white candles

name: The Downy Birch of the Flaucher
transport: 7 min walk from the Tierpark (Alemannenstraße) bus stop
story:
Downy birch is the last broadleaved tree before the tundra. Betula pubescens grows further north than any other, past the Arctic Circle in Scandinavia and across Iceland, and it manages it by staying quick, modest and short lived; a hundred years is a long run for one. Which makes Munich's reason for protecting this one worth reading twice: a mighty solitary tree, rare at this size in the city.

It stands in the Flaucher, the belt of gravel banks, pine and poplar along the Isar in the south of Munich where the city comes to swim and grill from May to September. That is the right ground for it. This is the wet-footed birch, the one that takes bogs, fens and river gravel where the silver birch cannot follow, and the fine hairs on its young twigs, the pubescens of the name, are how the two are told apart.

Birch bark is white for the same reason a roof is painted white. Betulin, the compound that makes the papery outer layer, reflects sunlight and keeps the trunk from warming and then splitting on cold bright days. It also burns when soaking wet, which is why birch bark has been lighting fires across northern Europe for as long as there have been fires to light.

The ordinance gives the reason for protection and no dimensions and no date, and nothing else has measured the tree.

name: The Ash of Leinthalerstraße
story:
Munich's ordinance gives three words for why this tree is protected: extrem ausladende Krone, an extremely wide-spreading crown. No size, no age, no history, nothing about the street. Just the shape, and it was enough.

The shape is also evidence. Fraxinus excelsior grown in a wood goes up tall and narrow, drawn on by its neighbours, and it only spreads when there is nothing beside it to compete with. A crown wide enough to earn a protection order on its own is a crown that grew in the open, and Freimann was farmland and village until Munich absorbed it in 1931. An ash does not spread like that in a street.

Ash is also the tree Europe is currently losing. A fungus from east Asia, harmless to the ashes it evolved alongside, reached Poland in the early 1990s and has been killing European ash ever since, blackening the leaves and thinning the crown from the top down. Some trees resist it and nobody yet knows how many, so a mature ash still carrying a full crown is not the ordinary sight it was thirty years ago.

The ordinance carries no dates and no measurements, and nothing else has recorded this tree, so its age is unknown. What is on the record is that in a list full of mighty and dominant trees, this one got in on width alone.

name: The Weeping Beech of Situlistraße
story:
By the city's own reckoning this is the largest weeping beech standing in Munich. The 2021 natural monument ordinance says so in its reason for protection, hedged with derzeit, currently, which is the honest way to make a superlative about something alive.

Every weeping beech is a graft. Fagus sylvatica 'Pendula' does not come true from seed, so each one is a cutting from the same weeping line joined onto the roots of an ordinary green beech, and on older specimens the union often still shows as a change in the bark near the ground. Above it the tree does what no wild beech does. The limbs arch outward and then fall, layer over layer, until the branch tips reach the ground and the whole crown closes into a room. Getting inside and standing at the trunk is the point of the species, and the reason gardeners have kept grafting it since the early nineteenth century.

It grows in the grounds at Situlistraße 73-75 in Freimann, about 70 metres from a copper beech the same ordinance protects on its own account, so the two are one short walk rather than two errands.

No age is recorded. The ordinance names reasons and never dates, so the city has written down that this is the biggest of its kind here without recording a single number about it.

name: The Copper Beech of Situlistraße
transport: 4 min walk from the Kulturheimstraße bus stop
story:
Purple leaves are a handicap. A copper beech is an ordinary beech carrying a mutation that floods its foliage with anthocyanin, which masks the chlorophyll underneath and cuts the light the leaf can actually put to work. In a wild forest that is a losing hand: purple seedlings are outgrown by green ones and vanish. The tree only exists in numbers because gardeners liked the colour and kept propagating what the forest would have discarded.

This is the second protected beech at Situlistraße 73-75 in Freimann. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance lists it separately from the weeping beech about 70 metres away, calling it a dominant tree that defines the local townscape and unique in the area, which for a document that mostly says mighty and dominant counts as enthusiasm.

What the ordinance does not list is a date, a girth or a height. It records reasons for protection and nothing else, and no other source has measured this tree, so the beech is documented in law and entirely undated.

The handicap gets paid off for about a fortnight a year. The new leaves open in late April and early May a thin luminous red you can see the sun through, then thicken and darken all summer towards something close to black. In August it is the heaviest looking thing on the street. In May it is the brightest.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves are thin enough to hold the sun behind them
